subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem: Read-Aloud and First Response

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud in full, stanza by stanza, with expressive voice — the morning hawker, the afternoon gardener, the evening watchman. Students follow in their textbooks (pp.105–107) and listen for the three workers and the time of day each appears.
Choral reading: the class reads the poem together aloud, with the teacher leading each stanza. Students focus on the refrain 'I wish I were…' and notice when it recurs.
Teacher asks a quick show-of-hands: which stanza did you find most vivid, and why? A few students share one observation each — no writing yet, just oral response.
Repeated reading: students read the poem independently and silently, then two volunteers read one stanza each aloud to close the sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: Tagore's poem moves through three times of day — morning, afternoon, dusk — and the child speaker admires each worker's apparent freedom from timetables. Students at this stage may need help with 'gong', 'spade', and 'lantern' — point to the words in context without stopping the rhythm of the reading. The simile 'a giant with one red eye' in stanza 3 often draws spontaneous comment; welcome it briefly.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: The Speaker and the Three Workers

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.108): answer questions about speaker, hawker, gardener, street lamp, daily schedule.

time_bands.activity: Brief re-recite: teacher and class chant the refrain 'I wish I were…' from each stanza together to bring the poem back into the room before discussion begins.
Let us Think — A., questions 1–3 (p.108): teacher poses each question aloud, students think-pair-share, then one pair shares with the class. Teacher confirms and extends answers from the poem's text.

Let us Think — A., questions 4–5 (p.108): question 4 focuses on the street-lamp simile; teacher invites students to describe what they picture. Question 5 asks students to reconstruct the speaker's day — teacher helps build a sequence: gong at ten, school, back at four, bed at dusk.
Students write brief answers to questions 1–4 in their notebooks independently. Teacher circulates and offers quiet prompts to students who are unsure.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together in the previous sitting, students now work closely with its content. The speaker's daily schedule (question 5) can be drawn as a simple timeline on the board — morning, afternoon, evening — which helps students who struggle to recall the poem's sequence. The simile of the street-lamp as 'a giant with one red eye' is the poem's most memorable image; linger on it briefly to build appreciation.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss: Admiring Different Vocations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.108): discuss why speaker admires vocations and personal observations on the way to school.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the first discussion question from Let us Think — B. (p.108): 'Why does the speaker admire people with different vocations?' Students think quietly, then share in pairs.

Pairs share their responses with the class; teacher records key ideas on the board — freedom, no fixed time, no one to scold, working outdoors. Teacher guides students to connect these ideas to the poem's theme of liberty versus rules.

Second discussion question (p.108): 'What are the things that you observe on your way to school and your way back home?' Students take turns describing a worker or scene they have noticed. Teacher prompts with: who, doing what, when, where.
Class comes together: teacher asks two or three students to share their favourite observation from the discussion and connects it to the poem's wistful tone — the child watching and wishing.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's central emotion is the child's longing to be free of school's timetable — each worker seems to move and rest at will. Students often conflate 'vocation' with 'job'; guide them toward the idea that a vocation is something a person does as their life's work. The second question is personal and experiential, so accept a wide range of observations warmly.

periods.activity_title: Group Question-Making: WH-Questions from the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.108): groups create and share WH-questions on the poem; other groups answer.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly reviews the WH-question words (who, what, when, where, why, how) on the board, giving one example from the poem: 'Where does the speaker see the gardener?'

Students sit in groups of five. Each group discusses the poem and writes two WH-questions about it. Teacher circulates, ensuring questions are about the poem's content and are answerable from the text.

Groups take turns presenting their questions to the class — textbooks placed in bags. The presenting group reads a question; the other groups answer aloud. Teacher moderates and affirms correct answers, gently correcting where needed.
Teacher highlights the two or three most interesting questions from the activity and briefly explains what made them strong — specific, tied to the poem's events.

periods.teacher_notes: This activity builds questioning skills alongside poem comprehension — students must understand the poem well enough to frame a question about it. Remind groups that their questions must be answerable from the poem's words, not from outside knowledge. If groups finish quickly, encourage them to refine their questions for precision.

periods.activity_title: Listen and Speak: Wanting Many Things at Once

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — B. (p.113): share a personal experience of wanting to do many things but being unable to.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the poem: the speaker wishes to be three different workers — hawker, gardener, watchman — all at once. Teacher models the speaking prompt by sharing a brief personal example of wanting to do several things simultaneously.

Students think quietly about a time they wanted to do many things but could not (Let us Speak — B., p.113): what they wanted to do, and what difficulties they faced. Students jot two or three words as memory prompts before speaking.
Students share in pairs, each taking a turn. Partner listens and asks one follow-up question: 'How did it make you feel?' Teacher moves around and listens, offering quiet encouragement.

Four or five students share their experiences with the whole class. Teacher summarises the common thread — the frustration and longing when we cannot do everything we wish — and links it back to the poem's wistful mood.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the poem's theme of longing in the previous discussions, students now connect it to their own lives. The speaking task requires personal reflection, so accept all genuine responses — there is no single correct answer. Students who are reluctant to speak may share in writing first and then read their sentences aloud.

periods.activity_title: Word Meanings and Grammar Errors: Poem Vocabulary and Sentence Correction

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.109): match five poem words — gong, spade, lane, giant, lantern — with their meanings.
Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110): identify and correct grammar errors in sentences 1–5.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110): correct sentences 6–10 independently at home.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn — A. (p.109): teacher writes the five words — gong, spade, lane, giant, lantern — on the board. Students find each word in the poem, read the line it appears in, and guess the meaning from context before checking the textbook's matching list. Class confirms each answer together.

Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110), sentences 1–5: teacher reads sentence 1 aloud and asks: 'What is wrong here?' Students identify the error, name the grammar point (verb agreement, preposition, comparison), and rewrite the correct sentence in their notebooks.
Students complete sentences 2–5 independently; teacher circulates. Class reviews answers together, with teacher explaining the grammar rule behind each correction concisely.
Teacher previews sentences 6–10 as the homework task, pointing out that they cover the same kinds of errors — students should name the mistake before rewriting.

periods.teacher_notes: Grounding word meanings in the poem's own lines (gong sounds ten, spade in the garden, lantern swinging) helps students retain them more durably than definitions alone. For the grammar correction task, the errors cover subject-verb agreement, prepositions, comparatives, and adverbs — resist giving the rule before students attempt to spot the error themselves.

periods.activity_title: Tools of the Trade and -tion Words: Vocabulary and Phonics

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.111): identify and discuss eleven labelled tool pictures — where seen, what used for.
Let us Speak — A. (p.112): listen-and-repeat drill for -tion/-sion words: cushion, ration, fashion, nation, vocation.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn — C. (p.111): teacher holds up the textbook showing the eleven labelled pictures — telescope, hammer, camera, screwdriver, sickle, stethoscope, grater, tongs, compass, mouse, saw. Students name each tool aloud, say where they might see it, and explain its use in one sentence.

Teacher links the tools to the poem's vocations: the hawker carries bangles, the gardener uses a spade. Students suggest which tool each illustrated worker might use and why — a quick oral game with light challenge.

Let us Speak — A. (p.112): teacher says each -tion/-sion word aloud — cushion, ration, fashion, tension, mention, attention, nation, vocation — and students repeat. Teacher draws attention to the shared ending sound /ʃən/ and asks students to clap on the final syllable.
Quick pair game: one student says a -tion word from the list, partner uses it in a sentence. Three or four pairs share with the class. Teacher confirms pronunciation and closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The tool vocabulary task connects to the poem's world of workers and instruments of labour — the spade has already appeared in the poem and anchors the discussion. The -tion/-sion drill prepares students to read and write 'vocation' with confidence; emphasise that 'vocation' (the chapter title) belongs to this same family of words.

periods.activity_title: Modelled Writing: The Difficult Side of a Job

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 1. (p.114): plan and write a paragraph on the difficult or boring side of the hawker's, gardener's, or watchman's job.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the poem's child-speaker, who sees only the fun side of each job — no timetable, no rules, no one to scold. Teacher asks: 'What might the hawker feel on a rainy day with no one buying?' Students offer ideas aloud before any writing begins.

Teacher models planning on the board: topic (the watchman at night), one difficulty, one boring aspect, one concluding thought. Students watch and take brief notes. Teacher then models drafting one sentence aloud and writes it, thinking out loud about word choice.

Students choose one worker — hawker, gardener, or watchman — and plan their paragraph in their notebooks (Let us Write — 1., p.114). Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with questions like 'What would happen if it rained?' or 'Would the watchman feel lonely?'
Students draft their paragraph. Teacher continues circulating and offers brief verbal feedback. Two volunteers read their paragraphs aloud and the class gives one positive observation each.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem presents each worker through the child's idealising eye, so this task asks students to think critically and imaginatively beyond the poem's surface. Accept a range of difficulties — physical hardship, weather, loneliness, low pay — as all are valid. Students who struggle to begin benefit most from the planning scaffold before drafting.

periods.activity_title: Writing About Family Vocations and Eminent Indians

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 2. (p.114): write 50–60 words on the vocations of three family members.
Let us Write — 3. (p.114): identify vocations of five eminent Indians — Kalam, Visvesvaraya, Janaki Ammal, Subbulakshmi, Salim Ali.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly discusses what a vocation means — a person's life work or calling — drawing on the word introduced in the poem. Students recall the poem's three workers and name their vocations aloud.

Let us Write — 2. (p.114): students choose three family members from the given list and write 50–60 words about each person's vocation. Teacher circulates and helps students who cannot decide what to write with guided questions: 'What does your mother do every day? What does she use?'

Let us Write — 3. (p.114): teacher writes the five names on the board — A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, M. Visvesvaraya, Janaki Ammal, M.S. Subbulakshmi, Salim Ali. Students discuss in pairs what they know about each, then write one sentence identifying the vocation of each person.

Class reviews the eminent Indians together — teacher confirms or supplies the vocation if students are unsure. Two or three students read one of their family-vocation paragraphs aloud to close the sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: Task 2 is personal and draws on students' home knowledge — accept any family member from the given list and any honest description of their work. For task 3, students at Grade V may not know all five figures; supply brief factual clues rather than answers directly — for example, 'one was India's missile scientist, one was a carnatic vocalist.'

periods.activity_title: Job Mix-Up! Spotting the Unusual in Vocation Pictures

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — Job Mix-Up! (p.115): study six pictures of professionals doing the wrong job and write two sentences per picture.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the activity: in each picture on p.115, a professional is doing another person's job. Teacher reads the example aloud: a chef driving a fire engine. Students identify the mix-up and say what each professional should really be doing.

Students study the remaining five pictures independently and note what is strange in each. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are unsure: 'What does a doctor normally do? What is this person doing instead?'

Students write two sentences per picture in their notebooks, following the example pattern: naming what the person is doing and naming what they should actually be doing. Teacher provides support with vocabulary as needed.

A few students share their sentences for one or two pictures aloud. Class confirms the correct vocation for each mixed-up professional and teacher closes with a brief reflection: vocations require specific skills and tools.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'Job Mix-Up' activity reinforces the concept of vocation through playful visual observation — it asks students to apply their understanding of what each profession actually involves. Students may need vocabulary for some professions shown (e.g. florist, architect, cobbler); supply these quickly in context rather than pausing the activity.

periods.activity_title: Let us Explore: Dream Vocations — Discussion and Drawing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore — A., B., C. (pp.117–118): choose a vocation, give reasons, discuss a dream job, draw yourself in it.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to look at the eight vocation illustrations on pp.116–117 — beekeeper, photographer, teacher, dancer, chef, pilot, farmer, florist — and name each one aloud. Students point to the one that interests them most without explaining yet.

Let us Explore — A. and B. (p.117): students discuss in pairs which illustrated vocation they would choose and why, then share whether there is a dream job not shown in the pictures. Teacher listens and invites three or four students to share with the whole class.

Let us Explore — C. (p.118): students draw themselves in their chosen vocation in the blank space provided. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to add details — tools, setting, clothing — that show what the vocation actually involves.

Students share their drawings with a partner and describe in one or two sentences what they drew. Teacher closes by connecting the activity to the poem: like the poem's speaker, we all imagine other lives and other kinds of freedom.

periods.teacher_notes: The exploration of dream vocations draws on the poem's central longing — the child's imagination of other lives — and invites students to name their own aspirations. Accept all vocations the students propose, including ones not on the illustrated list. The drawing task is expressive and should feel unhurried; students who finish quickly can add a label or caption to their picture.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 106 beginning "The lane is dark and lonely, and the street-lamp stands". What does the speaker compare the street lamp to, and what does this comparison tell us about how the speaker sees the night?

options.label: A
options.text: A tall tree with glowing leaves, suggesting the night is peaceful.

options.label: B
options.text: A giant with one red eye, suggesting the night feels mysterious and larger than life.

options.label: C
options.text: A lantern on a pole, suggesting the watchman hung it there himself.

options.label: D
options.text: A sleeping creature, suggesting the lane is completely silent.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be connecting the visual of light with nature rather than tracking the poem's specific simile.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has read 'lantern' and 'lamp' as the same object, missing the figurative language.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be responding to 'dark and lonely' without reading the simile that follows.

items.source_lo: Student infers and explains a poet's central ideas and imagery using a lyric poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Child speaker's longing for the hawker's, gardener's, and watchman's freedom; street-lamp simile; daily schedule.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the speaker watches three different workers across one day and wishes to be each of them. What is the ONE idea about freedom that connects all three wishes? Write one or two sentences to explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The speaker wishes to be free from timetables and rules — the hawker has no road he must take, the gardener has no one to stop him digging, and the watchman never goes to bed. Each worker seems to move and rest entirely at will, which is exactly what the schoolchild cannot do.

items.source_context: Why speaker admires each worker's freedom; personal observations on the way to school; WH-questions from the poem; wanting many things at once.
items.item_stem: Listen to your teacher read this description aloud: 'Every morning, a child hears the school gong and must hurry along the lane. Along the same lane, a hawker walks at his own pace, calling out his wares, with nowhere he must be.' Which of the following best describes why the child envies the hawker?

options.label: A
options.text: The hawker earns a lot of money selling bangles.

options.label: B
options.text: The hawker has no fixed time, road, or place he must go to.

options.label: C
options.text: The hawker gets to stay at home all morning.

options.label: D
options.text: The hawker is friends with the gardener and the watchman.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be thinking about the practical value of work rather than the poem's theme of freedom.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has confused 'no place he must go to' with staying home — a partial reading of the poem.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be guessing based on the presence of all three workers in the poem, rather than the reason given.

items.item_stem: Think of a time when you wanted to do two or three things at once but could not manage all of them. Tell your classmates: what did you want to do, what stopped you, and how did it make you feel? Speak in three or four sentences.

expected_elements: Names at least two things they wanted to do.
Identifies one reason they could not do both.
Describes a feeling — frustration, longing, or similar.

items.item_stem: The poem's speaker sees only the exciting side of the watchman's job — walking in the dark with a lantern, never going to bed. Write one sentence describing something difficult or tiring that the watchman's job might actually involve.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The watchman must stay awake through the entire night even when he is tired, walking the dark and lonely lane in all kinds of weather with no one to talk to.

items.item_stem: Choose one person from your family and write a short paragraph of four to five sentences about their vocation — what they do, what tools or skills they use, and why their work is important.

expected_elements: Names the family member and their vocation clearly.
Describes at least one task or tool of the job.
Explains why the work matters or helps others.
